memoryText: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read 1 Corinthians 13:13 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the last line of the love chapter, and it summarizes a chapter about what lasts.

“So now.” Paul has described gifts that will pass away: prophecies, tongues, knowledge. They are temporary scaffolding. “Now” marks the present time between Christ’s first and second comings.

“Faith, hope, and love abide.” These three remain. Faith trusts God’s promises. Hope looks forward to what he has promised. Love gives itself to God and others. Each is a gift of the Spirit, and each is fixed on Christ.

“These three.” They go together. Faith without love is dead; hope without faith is wishful; love without hope grows weary. The Christian life is a life of all three.

“But the greatest of these is love.” Why is love greatest? Because faith will become sight, and hope will be fulfilled, but love will last forever. God himself is love. In heaven, we won’t need to believe what we see or hope for what we have, but we will love for all eternity.

When you wonder what matters most in the church or in your life, say this verse. Love is the measure of all.
weekInReview: This week you read more of 1 Corinthians and saw how Paul answered a church’s questions with the gospel. In chapters 8 to 10, you learned how to use freedom: knowledge puffs up but love builds up, and whatever we do we should do for the glory of God. A doctrinal pause on the Lord’s Supper taught that Jesus gave his church a meal of remembrance, proclamation, and hope, and that we come in repentance and unity. In chapter 11, you read about order in worship and the sin of dividing the body at the Lord’s table. Chapters 12 to 14 gave the great teaching on spiritual gifts: one Spirit, many gifts, one body, and the more excellent way of love. A second doctrinal pause considered the gifts and the body of Christ. Psalm 111 called us to remember and give thanks for the works of the LORD, who sent redemption to his people.
reflectionQuestions: Paul says love is greater than faith and hope. What does it look like to treat love as the most important measure of your spiritual life, and not gifts, knowledge, or activity?
The Lord’s Supper proclaims Christ’s death until he comes. How might you prepare differently the next time you take Communion?
What gift has God given you for the common good of your church? Who in your church needs what you can offer?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for the meal of remembrance.
Thank him for gifts he gives his church.
Ask him to teach you to love as he loves.
